author: haiku
reason: B is better for a newcomer: it opens with a plain overview, defines the protocol terms that A takes as known (OIDC, PKCE, state, nonce, GETDEL, TTL), and explains the reasons behind its choices, such as the account invariants, why the cookie uses SameSite=Lax, and what happens when Redis is down, while A is tidier but assumes you already know the stack.

author: haiku
reason: A defines every term a newcomer needs, including OIDC, PKCE, state, nonce, GETDEL, TTL and the sid cookie. It also explains why things are built the way they are (the SameSite=Lax cookie, the no-password/no-link invariant, how parallel inserts are resolved) and covers what happens when Redis is down. B has neatly structured steps, but it assumes the reader already knows the protocol and leaves that Redis case open.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to pick up without knowing the project: it explains PKCE, state, nonce and GETDEL, sums the flow up in five steps before the details, and splits the flowchart into numbered, colour-coded sections with a guide on how to read them, while A assumes the reader already knows OAuth and sends every failure to a single BACK node whose messages sit in a separate table.

author: sonnet
reason: A is the one I would rather be handed as a newcomer: it defines PKCE, state, nonce and GETDEL, gives a numbered "in short" summary and ground rules, explains how to read the flowchart and its colours, and shows each outcome's message where it happens in the chart, while B assumes OAuth terms are known and sends every failure to a single BACK node, so you have to look up a separate table to see what the user is told.

author: haiku
reason: Document A is easier for a newcomer to follow because each step uses the same four fields (what starts it, what it does, which data it keeps, what happens on failure), and a single failure table backs them up. Document B explains more of its reasoning, but it spreads the same flow across topic-based notes and one very dense diagram.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow: it opens with a short summary, keeps its flowchart to the main load path, and walks through numbered steps that each say what starts the step, what it does, what data it keeps and what happens when it fails, then adds a failure table. A covers more ground (leases, snapshots, a proof of why the lookback is long enough), but it puts all of that into one dense diagram and a set of notes grouped by topic, so a reader has to piece the order of events together.

author: sonnet
reason: A is easier for a newcomer to follow: it lays the run out in three plainly named parts, defines every term it relies on (upsert, run lease, run_date), gives a table of where each piece of state lives, and shows the actual commit SQL, while B packs the same design into denser prose with fewer concrete anchors, even though its failure table covers more edge cases.

reason: For a newcomer, B is easier to follow: it defines the basic concepts A takes for granted (log partitions, offsets, the KV store's set-if-absent and TTL) and opens with the five decisions that shape everything, each with its reason, before the steps.

reason: B opens by describing how the page works today, then follows one request from click to download in runtime order and keeps build and rollout steps in their own section, so a newcomer gets the system model faster than from A, which mixes build tasks (refactor, migration) into its runtime steps and spreads the same content over more words.

reason: Document B is better for a newcomer: it opens with a plain overview and a map of which steps belong to which path, defines the replica, the primary and the "view", lists every name it proposes, gives its reasons (such as why the 2-hour orphan cutoff is safe and why status reads come from the primary), and ends with a table tying each requirement to the step that meets it, while Document A is tighter but explains less.

reason: B opens by describing how the reports page works today and labels each step with where it runs (browser, API server, worker), and its failure summary table gives a newcomer a clearer picture of the whole system than A, which is just as thorough but wordier.

reason: A starts with how the system works today, then follows each request in the same order as its diagram, with steps that say what triggers them and what they store, plus a failure table, and the three parts agree; B gives more rationale and a script, but it points to numbered requirements a newcomer never sees, shows the undecided Enterprise path going through a check that has no limit, and mixes the gateway's clock with Redis's clock, so it is harder to build an accurate picture from.

author: haiku
reason: A suits an outsider better: it defines the stack terms that B takes for granted (Redis primary and replica, Lua EVAL atomicity, TTL, load balancer, 401/429), explains why each design choice was made and which alternatives were rejected, and includes the actual script, so a newcomer can see the whole mechanism; B's step list and failure table are cleaner but leave more to prior knowledge.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts with how the gateway works today, then gives each decision with its reason, a clean diagram and a failure table I can scan, so I understand the system faster; B covers more mechanism detail, but it repeats itself and packs the script steps and headers into a heavy diagram.

author: sonnet
reason: A suits a reader who doesn't know the stack better: it defines Redis, Lua scripts and fail-open, explains how to read the diagram, and walks through the atomic script step by step, while B gives better context on the current system but assumes the reader already knows Redis and Lua.

author: haiku
reason: B gives a newcomer more to hold on to: it opens with a three-phase overview, defines more terms (replica, lease, epoch, idempotent, control row), and explains why it makes its choices, such as the 30 s flag cache, why the outbox avoids app.jobs and jobs:dead, and why pauses use control rows instead of flags. A assumes that context and mentions things like the Redis 5-retry cap and jobs:dead without explaining them.

author: haiku
reason: A starts with a three-phase overview and defines every term a newcomer would hit, including replica, lease, epoch and idempotent. It also explains why each design choice was made, and it defines the switch procedure once and reuses it for the cutover, the rollback and the finish, so the whole system is easier to keep in mind than B's flag-based steps and thinner glossary.

author: sonnet
reason: B is the easier of the two for a newcomer: its first section gives the whole idea in one place (one commit, quick copy and repair loop whose source and follower roles swap at the switch, which is what makes rollback possible), it explains why it uses fences and an outbox in a separate decisions section, and it groups the steps into named phases, while A packs its explanation into a dense terms list and sections that assume you already know how the parts fit together.

author: sonnet
reason: A gives a newcomer one clear mental model up front: commit with an outbox, a quick best-effort copy, then a drainer that repairs anything missed. It also explains that the same mechanism runs in reverse after the roles swap, so rollback makes sense before the steps start. B's 'How the system runs' section is useful, but its delete path, its fence wording ('the database this instance's mode expects') and its scattered caveats are harder to follow.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to understand: it states the two rules every step must keep up front, defines the basic terms (billing period, payment provider, and how the charge key works as the idempotency key), explains how to read the diagram and that the rollback boxes are not values of billing_mode, and says why each rollback path has the steps it does; A is terser and keeps pointing to "the brief", which a newcomer would not have.

author: haiku
reason: A is easier for a newcomer to follow: it defines every basic term (invoice, billing period, payment provider, and the charge key as the provider's idempotency key), explains how to read the diagram and that rollback steps are not flag values, and shows that rollback runs different steps from each starting mode. B mixes flag values with lifecycle states under "Modes", has thinner definitions, and keeps citing "the brief", which the reader has never seen.

author: sonnet
reason: B is better for a newcomer because it explains why the design works the way it does: the old engine skips events in new_only, so a rollback has to reprocess them, and the 35-day log retention is why rollback closes at day 35; it also defines more of the basic terms and lists every reconciliation outcome, while A is tighter but leaves more of that reasoning unstated.

author: sonnet
reason: A defines every system a newcomer needs up front (usage event log, ledger, payment provider, config service, controller), says what the diagram's conventions mean, explains why each rule exists, such as why the way back closes at day 35 and why a rollback from both needs no reprocessing, and lists the four concrete reconciliation outcomes; B's design is arguably stronger, but its steps, terms and diagram labels leave more for an outsider to infer.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to learn from: it starts with the four ways checkout can end, defines basic terms like service, event and outbox, walks through the flow in plain words, and labels its diagram boxes (O1, I1, P1) so a later section can cite them to show why the design is safe; A covers more edge cases, such as reconciliation and commit timeouts, but its broker-centred diagram is harder to follow and it relies on a "brief" the reader has never seen.

author: haiku
reason: A starts with the four ways a checkout can end, defines every term an outsider needs (service, event, outbox, claim, idempotency key, webhook), and ties its plain-words flow to diagram nodes labelled O1, I1, P1 and so on, then states the safety rules outright; B covers more edge cases, such as the reconcile timer, commit timeouts and a broker outage, but its terms are thinner and its diagram is harder to map back to the text.
